analysis.one_liner: Created a federal board to police corporate auditors and made top executives personally certify their companies' financial reports.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee in July 2002 and then to a subcommittee in August, never received a committee or floor vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Passed at the height of the Enron and WorldCom accounting scandals, this bill would have ended the system in which the auditing industry policed itself. It created a Public Company Accounting Oversight Board with power to register, inspect, and discipline the firms that audit public companies. It banned auditors from selling lucrative consulting services to the companies they audit, required CEOs and CFOs to personally certify financial statements and forfeit bonuses after a fraudulent restatement, barred executives from trading their own company stock during the blackout periods when employees' 401(k) accounts are frozen, and required disclosure of the off-balance-sheet deals and executive loans that had hidden Enron's losses.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors and workers whose savings and retirement accounts depend on honest corporate financial reporting. The bill's own statement of purpose says it exists to protect the interests of public investors and further the public interest in accurate, independent audit reports [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, with SEC oversight, that would register public accounting firms, conduct inspections, and impose sanctions including fines of up to $15 million on firms that violate auditing rules [S2][S3].

Prohibits an audit firm from performing non-audit services like bookkeeping, systems design, and valuation work for a company it is simultaneously auditing — the conflict that had let Enron's auditor approve shaky books while collecting consulting fees [S2][S3].
Requires CEOs and CFOs to certify the accuracy of mandatory financial statements and to forfeit bonuses and compensation received before an accounting restatement [S2][S3].

Prohibits insider trades during pension fund blackout periods, when 401(k) participants are locked out of selling but executives are not, and mandates disclosure of off-balance-sheet transactions and loans and guarantees to senior executives [S2][S3].

Requires five-year rotation of audit partners, bars auditors whose senior executives recently worked for the company they audit, and mandates SEC rules to clean up conflicts of interest among stock analysts [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public companies and their executives, and the large public accounting firms. Companies pay a share of the oversight board's budget through an annual fee allocated by market capitalization [S3]. Audit firms lose the right to sell consulting services to their own audit clients, face registration fees, inspections, and fines, and executives face certification, bonus forfeiture, and trading bans [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real and are ultimately borne by shareholders and consumers: every public company must pay a share of the oversight board's budget and the standard-setter's budget, allocated by market capitalization [S3].

The oversight board is deliberately structured as a private nonprofit corporation rather than a government agency, with most of its operations shielded from public disclosure, including confidential investigations and hearings held behind closed doors [S3].

The ban on non-audit services and the personal certification and forfeiture rules raise audit prices and can make it harder to recruit qualified executives and auditors, and honest supporters would acknowledge that some of these costs fall on companies that never fudge their books.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are compliance expenses paid by companies that are already required to file accurate financial statements, while the benefit is a check on a self-policing audit industry that had, in the Enron and WorldCom cases, certified books that later proved false and wiped out employee retirement savings. The bill is also less sweeping than critics demanded in some respects — it studies but does not require rotating audit firms themselves, and it lets the board grant exemptions — so it is a genuine reform with meaningful, but not extreme, costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee on August 19, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended; Congress instead passed a competing corporate-accountability bill (the Sarbanes-Oxley Act) later that same month.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce (D-NY) introduced the bill on July 9, 2002, joined on introduction by Reps. Dingell and Gephardt [S3][S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day it was introduced [S5].
On August 19, 2002, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises [S5].
The complete action history shows no further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because Congress passed a competing version with most of the same core safeguards (Sarbanes-Oxley) weeks later, investors did not lose everything. But the vehicle Congress actually chose was the House Republican leadership's bill rather than this one, so large accounting firms and public companies got the new rules through a process their allies controlled, and they avoided any provisions unique to the tougher competing drafts.

for.name: Rep. John LaFalce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create an independent board to police corporate auditors and tighten executive accountability.

for.name: Reps. John Dingell and Richard Gephardt
for.role: House members who joined on introduction
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as original sponsors [S3].

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Michael Oxley)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on August 19 and never scheduled a markup or vote; the complete action history ends there [S5].

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Moved its own competing corporate-reform bill instead of this one, which never reached the floor.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the toughest investor-restitution provisions in the competing Senate bill and backed the House Republican version.

sides.party_line_note: All six cosponsors were House Democrats, and the Republican majority advanced its own version instead; the competing corporate-accountability law that passed both chambers weeks later did so with near-unanimous votes (97-0 in the Senate, 423-3 in the House).

industries.note: The bill forces audit firms to register with and answer to a new oversight board with inspection and sanction powers, bans them from selling consulting services to their own audit clients, and charges them fees — eliminating revenue streams that had flowed precisely because auditors also served as paid consultants to the companies they certified.

CEOs and CFOs must personally certify financial statements, forfeit bonuses after a fraudulent restatement, disclose executive loans, and stop trading during pension blackout periods — the personal accountability the Enron and WorldCom cases showed was missing.

Companies bear an annual fee for the oversight board and standard-setter, audit committee oversight requirements, and enhanced disclosure of off-balance-sheet deals — compliance costs that are the direct price of the investor protections the bill provides.

The bill mandates SEC rules governing analyst conflicts of interest and requires brokers to consider analyst qualifications — aimed at the practice of banks using flattering analyst reports to win underwriting business from companies whose stocks analysts covered.
